procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 03.02.2010 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in CRLA No.1982 of 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants made separate applications for discharge, but the learned Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate rejected the applications. A revision application preferred against the order of rejection, was also dismissed. Being aggrieved by the said order, an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short, ‘Cr.PC’) was ﬁ led by the appellants which has been dismissed by the impugned judgment dated 3rd February 2010 by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Bombay.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants, feeling aggrieved by the High Court's order, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

directions: The Trial Court is directed to give necessary out-of-turn priority to the disposal of the complaint bearing CC.No.14/CW/2002.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Enforcement Officer appointed under FERA, 1973 continued to have the authority or competence to file a complaint for the offences punishable under FERA before the expiry of the sunset period provided in sub-section (3) of s.49 of FEMA, 1999.

facts: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (FERA) was repealed and replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) with effect from June 1, 2000.
A complaint for an offence under the repealed FERA was filed by an Enforcement Officer who had been appointed under FERA.
The complaint was filed and the court took cognizance of it within the two-year 'sunset period' provided by Section 49(3) of FEMA, which allowed for the prosecution of old FERA offences.
law: Section 49(3) of FEMA provides a two-year 'sunset period' after the repeal of FERA, during which courts can take cognizance of offences committed under the old Act.

Section 49(4) of FEMA states that, subject to the sunset period in sub-section (3), all offences committed under the repealed FERA shall continue to be governed by the provisions of FERA 'as if that Act had not been repealed'.
Section 61(2) of FERA specified that only an authorized officer, such as an Enforcement Officer, could file a complaint for FERA offences.
application: The Court identified Section 49(4) of FEMA as the key provision to resolve the issue.

It interpreted this section as creating a 'legal fiction'. This means that for the specific purpose of prosecuting offences saved by the sunset clause, the entire legal framework of the repealed FERA is treated as if it were still in effect.

Because of this legal fiction, the provisions of FERA that empowered and authorized Enforcement Officers to file complaints (like Section 3 and Section 61) also continued to be valid for prosecutions initiated during the sunset period.

The Court reasoned that if the Enforcement Officer's authority was not saved, then no one would be competent to file a complaint during the two-year sunset period. This would render the saving provision in Section 49(3) of FEMA meaningless and unworkable ('otiose').
The Court concluded that an interpretation that defeats the plain intention of the legislature must be rejected, and the law must be interpreted in a way that makes its provisions workable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument that the Enforcement Officer continued to have the authority to file the complaint. It held that due to the legal fiction created by Section 49(4) of FEMA, the provisions of the repealed FERA, including the authority of its officers, remained in force for the limited purpose of prosecuting offences within the two-year sunset period provided by Section 49(3).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Enforcement Officer appointed under FERA, 1973 continued to have the authority or competence to file a complaint for the offences punishable under FERA before the expiry of the sunset period provided in sub-section (3) of s.49 of FEMA, 1999.
appellant_arguments: Based on the procedural history, the appellants sought discharge from the case, arguing that the complaint was not maintainable. This implies their argument was that the Enforcement Officer, appointed under the repealed FERA, 1973, lost the authority and competence to file a complaint after FERA was repealed by FEMA, 1999. The repeal of the Act meant the machinery for its enforcement ceased to exist, and the savings clause in FEMA was insufficient to grant the officer the power to initiate a new complaint.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, which was upheld by the courts, would have been that the savings clause in Section 49(3) of FEMA, 1999, specifically preserved the authority of the Enforcement Officer to investigate and file complaints for offences committed when FERA was in force. This authority was explicitly saved for the duration of the two-year "sunset period" provided in the statute, allowing for the continuation of legal action for past violations.

cases.case_name: M/s. P.V. Mohammad Barmay Sons v. Director of Enforcement
cases.principle: Unless a contrary intention is manifested in a new repealing Act, the liabilities, penalties, forfeiture, or punishment incurred under the repealed Act will continue to exist and remain in force by operation of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act. The right to investigate or take legal proceedings for actions done under the repealed act remains unaffected and preserved.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In the absence of a contrary intention in a repealing statute, Section 6(d) of the General Clauses Act applies to preserve the liability for any penalty, forfeiture, or punishment for an offense committed under the repealed enactment, even if criminal proceedings were not initiated before the repeal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the repeal of an enactment does not extinguish the liability or punishment for an offence committed before the repeal. Relying on Section 6(d) of the General Clauses Act and the precedent set in M/s. P.V. Mohammad Barmay Sons, the court held that criminal proceedings for past offences can be initiated after the repeal, as long as the new repealing act does not show a contrary intention.
legal_tests_applied: Section 6(d) of the General Clauses Act: This section provides that the repeal of an enactment shall not affect any penalty, forfeiture, or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against the repealed enactment, and any such investigation, legal proceeding, or remedy may be instituted, continued, or enforced as if the repealing Act had not been passed.

The 'Contrary Intention' Test: The application of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act is subject to whether a contrary intention appears in the new repealing statute. The court found that the new Act did not evince any such contrary intention.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the Enforcement Officer's authority ceased with the repeal of FERA was rejected because it failed to account for the legal effect of Section 6(d) of the General Clauses Act.
The court found, based on precedent, that the new Act (FEMA) did not express a 'contrary intention' that would prevent the initiation of proceedings for offences committed under the old Act (FERA).
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because it aligned with the established principle that Section 6(d) of the General Clauses Act preserves the ability to initiate criminal proceedings for offences committed under a repealed law, even if those proceedings had not been started before the repeal.

The court's reasoning was directly 'fortified' by the decision in M/s. P.V. Mohammad Barmay Sons, which held that penalties and punishments for offences committed under a repealed act remain enforceable.
policy_considerations: The underlying principle is to ensure legal continuity and prevent offenders from escaping liability simply due to the repeal and replacement of a statute. The application of the General Clauses Act ensures that penalties and punishments for offences already committed are not nullified by subsequent legislative changes, unless the legislature explicitly intends such an outcome.
